newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela slams South African prophets of doom.
newsitem.headline: Mandela slams South African prophets of doom.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela criticised on Wednesday prophets of doom in his country and said South Africa's recovery after decades of white rule would take time and hard work.
Mandela, who on Tuesday said cracks were showing in South Africa's post-apartheid unity, called for a renewed commitment to reconciliation and reconstruction.
"There is no magic wand to rectify the problems we face and we should avoid...the tendency to pronounce imminent doom in the face of obstacles in our way.
"Change, fundamental change, requires a long hard slog and we will go through tortuous paths and difficulties before we reach the mountain tops," he said.

Closing an annual two-day parliamentary debate on his presidency, Mandela defended his government's efforts to restructure the civil service to correct the pro-white racial imbalance inherited from apartheid.
He said affirmative action in favour of the black majority need not mean a drop in standards.
Mandela indirectly criticised former president F.W. de Klerk's role in the search for unity and reconciliation.
"Reconciliation also means that leaders should lead by example in acknowledging mistakes of the past and committing themselves to prevent their repetition.

"Indeed, brave men and women of the current age will be found at the forefront of reconciliation efforts, assisting the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and not holding back their supporters from taking part in its work or abandoning those who served under them," he said.

De Klerk has said repeatedly that the Truth Commission, headed by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, singles out white Afrikaners and does not focus equally on human rights crimes by members of Mandela's African National Congress during the war against apartheid.
He has dismissed evidence of widespread torture and assassination as the work of rogue policemen and soldiers and has insisted he knew nothing about their work and has no reason to feel guilty.
Mandela said everyone should participate in the search for reconciliation and forgiveness.
"It means recognising the sacrifices of millions of poor people at the same time as we accommodate those who directly or by proxy perpetuated apartheid," he said.
